claim: Genetic mutation, chromosomal rearrangement and copy number amplification are common mechanisms responsible for generating gain-of-function, cancer-causing alterations.
source: Genetic mutation, chromosomal rearrangement and copy number amplification are common mechanisms responsible for generating gain-of-function, cancer-causing alterations.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cancer mechanisms.

claim: Premature cleavage and polyadenylation (pPA) of RNA can produce an oncogenic protein.
source: Here we report a new mechanism by which premature cleavage and polyadenylation (pPA) of RNA can produce an oncogenic protein.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A pPA event occurs at a cryptic intronic poly(A) signal in MAGI3 in the absence of local exonic and intronic mutations.
source: We identify a pPA event at a cryptic intronic poly(A) signal in MAGI3, occurring in the absence of local exonic and intronic mutations.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data showing no mutations in the relevant regions (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).

claim: The altered mRNA isoform MAGI3pPA produces a truncated protein that acts in a dominant-negative manner.
source: The altered mRNA isoform, called MAGI3pPA, produces a truncated protein that acts in a dominant-negative manner to prevent full-length MAGI3 from interacting with the YAP oncoprotein, thereby relieving YAP inhibition and promoting malignant transformation of human mammary epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and transformation assays shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: MAGI3pPA prevents full-length MAGI3 from interacting with the YAP oncoprotein.
source: The altered mRNA isoform, called MAGI3pPA, produces a truncated protein that acts in a dominant-negative manner to prevent full-length MAGI3 from interacting with the YAP oncoprotein, thereby relieving YAP inhibition and promoting malignant transformation of human mammary epithelial cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments in Figure 6A showing that truncated MAGI3 prevents endogenous full-length MAGI3 from interacting with YAP.

claim: MAGI3pPA relieves YAP inhibition and promotes malignant transformation of human mammary epithelial cells.
source: The altered mRNA isoform, called MAGI3pPA, produces a truncated protein that acts in a dominant-negative manner to prevent full-length MAGI3 from interacting with the YAP oncoprotein, thereby relieving YAP inhibition and promoting malignant transformation of human mammary epithelial cells.
evidence: This is supported by transformation assays (Figure 3) and YAP activation data (Figure 5).

claim: MAGI3pPA is recurrently expressed in primary human breast tumors but not in tumor-adjacent normal tissues.
source: We additionally find evidence for recurrent expression of MAGI3pPA in primary human breast tumors but not in tumor-adjacent normal tissues.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-Seq analysis of 160 primary breast tumors and 160 matched normal samples (Figure 2).

claim: Many tumors harbor alterations in only 1–2 known drivers.
source: Interestingly, results from these analyses indicate that many tumors harbor alterations in only 1–2 known drivers, and ~15% of tumors lack alterations in even a single known driver (Imielinski et al., 2012; Garraway and Lander, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Approximately 15% of tumors lack alterations in even a single known driver.
source: Interestingly, results from these analyses indicate that many tumors harbor alterations in only 1–2 known drivers, and ~15% of tumors lack alterations in even a single known driver (Imielinski et al., 2012; Garraway and Lander, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Solid tumors arise due to oncogenic cooperation between alterations in multiple drivers.
source: Since solid tumors arise due to oncogenic cooperation between alterations in multiple drivers (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990; Hanahan and Weinberg, 2000), a significant number of cancer-relevant genes are currently being missed by genomic analyses because so many genes are ostensibly altered at frequencies below the threshold for driver detection (Lawrence et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in cancer biology, supported by citations.

claim: A truncated MAGI3 protein is expressed in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells.
source: A truncated MAGI3 protein (indicated by red asterisks) is expressed in MDA-MB-231 cells.
evidence: This is shown by immunoblot in Figure 1B.

claim: The truncated MAGI3 protein in MDA-MB-231 cells is not expressed in non-transformed MCF10A mammary cell line or TERT-immortalized human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC).
source: Notably, this truncation was not expressed in the non-transformed MCF10A mammary cell line or TERT-immortalized human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC) (Figure 1B and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data in Figure 1B and D.

claim: MAGI3 is a scaffolding protein with 2 WW and 6 PDZ domains, along with a catalytically inactive region of homology to the yeast guanylate kinase.
source: MAGI3 is a scaffolding protein with 2 WW and 6 PDZ domains, along with a catalytically inactive region of homology to the yeast guanylate kinase (Figure 1E) (Funke et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MAGI3 protein structure, supported by citation and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of the truncated MAGI3 protein mapped many peptides corresponding to the N-terminal half of MAGI3, but detected no peptides from the PDZ domains 3–6 that consist of the C-terminal half of MAGI3.
source: Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of the immunoprecipitated truncation mapped many peptides corresponding to the N-terminal half of MAGI3, but detected no peptides from the PDZ domains 3–6 that consist of the C-terminal half of MAGI3 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Sequencing of all 22 exons and flanking intron sequences of MAGI3 found no mutations in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: To identify the genetic alteration responsible for this truncation, we sequenced all 22 exons and flanking intron sequences of MAGI3 but found no mutations.
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The truncation of MAGI3 is not generated by DNA mutation of the MAGI3 coding sequence or splice sites.
source: This indicated that the truncation is not generated by DNA mutation of the MAGI3 coding sequence or splice sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data showing no mutations.

claim: 3′ RACE sequencing revealed a cleavage and polyadenylation event involving a cryptic poly(A) signal (PAS) located in MAGI3 intron 10.
source: Sequencing the 3′ end of the mRNA revealed a cleavage and polyadenylation event involving a cryptic poly(A) signal (PAS) located in MAGI3 intron 10 (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by 3′ RACE sequencing data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: The normal splicing event from exon 10 to exon 11 of MAGI3 does not occur in the truncated mRNA (MAGI3pPA).
source: Consequently, the normal splicing event from exon 10 to exon 11 of MAGI3 does not occur in the truncated mRNA (MAGI3pPA), resulting in a stop codon several nucleotides into intron 10 and premature transcription termination following the cryptic intronic PAS (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 1H.

claim: MAGI3pPA results in a stop codon several nucleotides into intron 10 and premature transcription termination following the cryptic intronic PAS.
source: Consequently, the normal splicing event from exon 10 to exon 11 of MAGI3 does not occur in the truncated mRNA (MAGI3pPA), resulting in a stop codon several nucleotides into intron 10 and premature transcription termination following the cryptic intronic PAS (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown by sequencing data in Figure 1H.

claim: The entire MAGI3 intron 10 from MDA-MB-231 cells contains no mutations.
source: Therefore, we sequenced the entire MAGI3 intron 10 from MDA-MB-231 cells but were unable to find any mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The entire region of the MAGI3pPA 3′ RACE product corresponding to intron 10 and the flanking exon 10 sequence contains no mutations.
source: We also sequenced the entire region of the MAGI3pPA 3′ RACE product corresponding to intron 10 and the flanking exon 10 sequence, but again uncovered no mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by sequencing data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cis-acting sequences involved in proper splicing and repression of pPA, including the upstream/downstream splice donors, upstream U1 snRNA binding site and downstream URE, were intact in MAGI3.
source: Notably, the known cis-acting sequences involved in proper splicing and repression of pPA, including the upstream/downstream splice donors, upstream U1 snRNA binding site and downstream URE, were intact in the sequencing analyses (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequencing data in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The pPA event in intron 10 of MAGI3 arises independently of local genetic mutations.
source: We thus conclude that this pPA event in intron 10 of MAGI3 arises independently of local genetic mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequencing data showing no mutations in the relevant regions.

claim: RNA-Seq data from TCGA and a previously published study included 160 primary breast tumors along with 160 matched, tumor-adjacent normal samples.
source: In total, these data included 160 primary breast tumors along with 160 matched, tumor-adjacent normal samples.
evidence: This describes the dataset used for analysis.

claim: The sequencing depth of MAGI3 between tumor and normal RNA-Seq data was comparable, with only a 1.1-fold median increase in tumor samples.
source: Since large differences in MAGI3 sequencing depth between the two sets of samples might bias detection of pPA events, we first compared sequencing depth of MAGI3 between tumor and normal RNA-Seq data and found it to be comparable, with only a 1.1-fold median increase in tumor samples.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-Seq data.

claim: The vast majority of tumor-adjacent normal samples (157 out of 160) had either no intronic reads or a few, isolated reads in MAGI3 intron 10.
source: The vast majority of tumor-adjacent normal samples (157 out of 160) had either no intronic reads or a few, isolated reads; only three samples exhibited long stretches of overlapping intronic reads (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only three tumor-adjacent normal samples exhibited long stretches of overlapping intronic reads in MAGI3 intron 10.
source: The vast majority of tumor-adjacent normal samples (157 out of 160) had either no intronic reads or a few, isolated reads; only three samples exhibited long stretches of overlapping intronic reads (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A larger fraction of primary tumors (26 out of 160) were observed with extended stretches of overlapping MAGI3 intron 10 reads.
source: In comparison, a larger fraction of primary tumors (26 out of 160) were observed with extended stretches of overlapping MAGI3 intron 10 reads (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Twelve tumor samples displayed continuous read signals across the pPA region and were considered to express the MAGI3pPA isoform.
source: We considered the remaining twelve tumor samples, displaying continuous read signals across the pPA region (Figure 2B), to express the MAGI3pPA isoform.
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The relative expression levels of the truncated MAGI3pPA isoform was between 2% to 6% of MAGI3α expression levels.
source: The relative expression levels of the truncated isoform was between 2% to 6% of MAGI3α expression levels, but was generally higher than or comparable to MAGI3β expression levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The relative expression levels of the truncated MAGI3pPA isoform was generally higher than or comparable to MAGI3β expression levels.
source: The relative expression levels of the truncated isoform was between 2% to 6% of MAGI3α expression levels, but was generally higher than or comparable to MAGI3β expression levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The MAGI3 pPA event occurs in 7.5% (12 out of 160) of primary breast tumors.
source: The occurrence of the MAGI3 pPA event in 7.5% (12 out of 160) of primary breast tumors and the absence of this event in matched tumor-adjacent normal tissues (0 out of 160) suggest that it is a tumor-specific and recurrent event that may play an important role in breast cancer pathogenesis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: The MAGI3 pPA event is absent in matched tumor-adjacent normal tissues (0 out of 160).
source: The occurrence of the MAGI3 pPA event in 7.5% (12 out of 160) of primary breast tumors and the absence of this event in matched tumor-adjacent normal tissues (0 out of 160) suggest that it is a tumor-specific and recurrent event that may play an important role in breast cancer pathogenesis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-Seq analysis summarized in Figure 2C.

claim: The MAGI3 pPA event is a tumor-specific and recurrent event.
source: The occurrence of the MAGI3 pPA event in 7.5% (12 out of 160) of primary breast tumors and the absence of this event in matched tumor-adjacent normal tissues (0 out of 160) suggest that it is a tumor-specific and recurrent event that may play an important role in breast cancer pathogenesis (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-Seq data showing occurrence in tumors but not normal tissues.

claim: Depletion of MAGI3pPA in MDA-MB-231 cells impaired the growth of cells on soft agar compared to non-silencing control.
source: Intriguingly, the loss of MAGI3pPA impaired the growth of MDA-MB-231 cells on soft agar compared to non-silencing Scr control, as shown by the reduced size and number of colonies (p=1.1 x 10–4 and 3.4 x 10–5 for shMAGI3.4 and shMAGI3.5, respectively) (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The MAGI3 intron 10 pPA event may have been positively selected by MDA-MB-231 cells during the process of malignant transformation.
source: These data suggest that the MAGI3 intron 10 pPA event may have been positively selected by MDA-MB-231 cells during the process of malignant transformation, and thus implicate pPA as a mechanism of alteration capable of contributing to breast cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional data showing that MAGI3pPA depletion impairs transformation.

claim: A MAGI3-AKT3 fusion gene, caused by a chromosomal rearrangement involving breakpoints at MAGI3 intron 9 and AKT3 intron 1, has been previously identified in breast cancer.
source: A MAGI3-AKT3 fusion gene, caused by a chromosomal rearrangement involving breakpoints at MAGI3 intron 9 and AKT3 intron 1, has been previously identified in breast cancer (Banerji et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a published study.

claim: MAGI3ΔC-GFP significantly promoted anchorage-independent growth on soft agar compared to control MCF10A-SV40 cells expressing GFP.
source: When ectopically expressed along with the SV40 early region in MCF10A cells (MCF10A-SV40), MAGI3ΔC-GFP significantly promoted anchorage-independent growth on soft agar compared to the poor growth of control MCF10A-SV40 cells expressing GFP (p=4.8 x 10–5) (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays shown in Figure 3F and G.

claim: Truncated MAGI3 products, whether generated by pPA or other alteration mechanisms, promote mammary cell transformation.
source: Together, these results suggest that truncated MAGI3 products, whether generated by pPA or other alteration mechanisms, promote mammary cell transformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the transformation assays with MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC-GFP.

claim: The kinase domain of MAGI3 lacks catalytic activity.
source: Because the kinase domain of MAGI3 lacks catalytic activity (Funke et al., 2005), we focused on identifying MAGI3 protein interactors by affinity purification of V5-tagged, full-length MAGI3 in MCF10A cells followed by mass spectrometry (AP-MS).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The YAP oncoprotein was identified as a top candidate interactor with MAGI3 by affinity purification-mass spectrometry.
source: The YAP oncoprotein – a transcription co-activator that functions as a major effector of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway – was identified to be top candidate interactor with MAGI3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on AP-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: YAP is a transcription co-activator that functions as a major effector of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway.
source: The YAP oncoprotein – a transcription co-activator that functions as a major effector of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway – was identified to be top candidate interactor with MAGI3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about YAP function.

claim: SERPINB5 (Maspin) was identified as a likely MAGI3 interactor by affinity purification-mass spectrometry.
source: SERPINB5, also known as the mammary tumor suppressor Maspin, was also identified as a likely MAGI3 interactor (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on AP-MS data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Several tight junction and cellular adhesion molecules were identified as MAGI3 interactors by affinity purification-mass spectrometry.
source: In addition, several tight junction and cellular adhesion molecules were identified by this analysis (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1), validating the AP-MS approach since MAGI3 has been observed to localize to cell junctions (Adamsky et al., 2003; Funke et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on AP-MS data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: MAGI3 has been observed to localize to cell junctions.
source: In addition, several tight junction and cellular adhesion molecules were identified by this analysis (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 1), validating the AP-MS approach since MAGI3 has been observed to localize to cell junctions (Adamsky et al., 2003; Funke et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: MAGI3 localizes to tight junctions in luminal cells and to the cytoplasm in basal/myoepithelial cells in human breast epithelium.
source: Indeed, the subcellular localization of MAGI3 in human breast epithelium is consistent with these previous reports, with tight junction localization in luminal cells and cytoplasmic localization in basal/myoepithelial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous YAP co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous MAGI3 from MCF10A cell lysates.
source: Indeed, we found that YAP co-immunoprecipitated with MAGI3 and likewise, MAGI3 co-immunoprecipitated with YAP from MCF10A cell lysates (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Endogenous MAGI3 co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous YAP from MCF10A cell lysates.
source: Indeed, we found that YAP co-immunoprecipitated with MAGI3 and likewise, MAGI3 co-immunoprecipitated with YAP from MCF10A cell lysates (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Flag-tagged full-length YAP co-immunoprecipitated with V5-tagged MAGI3 in HEK293T cells.
source: Consistent with the endogenous co-IP results, Flag-tagged full-length YAP co-immunoprecipitated with V5-tagged MAGI3 in HEK293T cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Flag-YAPΔC and MAGI3-V5 could not be co-immunoprecipitated by either anti-Flag or anti-V5 IP.
source: However, Flag-YAPΔC and MAGI3-V5 could not be co-immunoprecipitated by either anti-Flag or anti-V5 IP (Figure 4C), indicating that the PDZ-binding motif of YAP is necessary for the physical interaction between the two proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The PDZ-binding motif of YAP is necessary for the physical interaction between YAP and MAGI3.
source: However, Flag-YAPΔC and MAGI3-V5 could not be co-immunoprecipitated by either anti-Flag or anti-V5 IP (Figure 4C), indicating that the PDZ-binding motif of YAP is necessary for the physical interaction between the two proteins.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP experiments showing that deletion of the PDZ-binding motif abolishes interaction.

claim: The sixth PDZ domain (PDZ6) of MAGI3 was the highest-scoring interactor with the PDZ-binding peptide of YAP according to computational prediction.
source: To further confirm that the interaction between YAP and MAGI3 requires PDZ domain-binding, we first utilized a computational predictor to map the PDZ-binding peptide of YAP against all human PDZ domains (Hui and Bader, 2010) and found that the sixth PDZ domain (PDZ6) of MAGI3 was the highest-scoring interactor on the list (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction results shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Deletion of PDZ6 curtailed MAGI3 interaction with YAP.
source: Deletion of PDZ6 curtailed MAGI3 interaction with YAP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The PDZ-binding motif of YAP and the PDZ6 domain of MAGI3 are necessary for protein-protein interaction.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that the PDZ-binding motif of YAP and the PDZ6 domain of MAGI3 are necessary for protein-protein interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP experiments with deletion mutants.

claim: Depletion of MAGI3 by RNAi in MCF10A cells induced the expression of YAP target genes ANKRD1 and CYR61.
source: When MCF10A cells were depleted of MAGI3 by RNAi, the expression of YAP target genes ANKRD1 and CYR61 were induced (p=9.9 x 10 –3 and 2.5 x 10–4, respectively), as determined by quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Rescue of MAGI3 levels restored the expression of ANKRD1 and CYR61 to baseline levels.
source: The rescue of MAGI3 levels restored the expression of ANKRD1 and CYR61 to baseline levels (p=0.012 and 3.5 x 10–4, respectively) (Figure 4E), thus demonstrating the specificity of YAP regulation by MAGI3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of MAGI3 in MCF10A-SV40 cells causes anchorage-independent growth.
source: Because RNAi-mediated knockdown of MAGI3 in MCF10A-SV40 cells causes anchorage-independent growth (p=1.4 x 10–3) (Figure 4F and G), and overexpression of YAP in MCF10A cells also causes transformation (Overholtzer et al., 2006), we used the transformed phenotype to conduct epistasis analysis between MAGI3 and YAP1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Overexpression of YAP in MCF10A cells causes transformation.
source: Because RNAi-mediated knockdown of MAGI3 in MCF10A-SV40 cells causes anchorage-independent growth (p=1.4 x 10–3) (Figure 4F and G), and overexpression of YAP in MCF10A cells also causes transformation (Overholtzer et al., 2006), we used the transformed phenotype to conduct epistasis analysis between MAGI3 and YAP1.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Knockdown of YAP1 in MAGI3-depleted cells restored the normal phenotype.
source: Knockdown of YAP1 in MAGI3-depleted cells restored the normal phenotype (p=4.9 x 10–5 and 8.9 x 10–4 for shYAP1 #1 and #2, respectively), as did restoring MAGI3 expression in MAGI3-depleted cells (p=6.5 x 10–7 and 2.0 x 10–5 for MAGI3α and MAGI3β, respectively) (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Restoring MAGI3 expression in MAGI3-depleted cells restored the normal phenotype.
source: Knockdown of YAP1 in MAGI3-depleted cells restored the normal phenotype (p=4.9 x 10–5 and 8.9 x 10–4 for shYAP1 #1 and #2, respectively), as did restoring MAGI3 expression in MAGI3-depleted cells (p=6.5 x 10–7 and 2.0 x 10–5 for MAGI3α and MAGI3β, respectively) (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: The protein-protein interaction between MAGI3 and YAP is physiologically relevant for the negative regulation of YAP by full-length MAGI3.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that the protein-protein interaction between MAGI3 and YAP is physiologically relevant for the negative regulation of YAP by full-length MAGI3.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiments and YAP target gene expression data.

claim: YAP activity exhibits highly robust responses to serum deprivation and subsequent serum stimulation in HEK293T cells.
source: In HEK293T cells, YAP activity exhibits highly robust responses to serum deprivation, which promotes cytoplasmic accumulation of YAP, and subsequent serum stimulation, which rapidly induces YAP nuclear translocation (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Serum deprivation promotes cytoplasmic accumulation of YAP.
source: In HEK293T cells, YAP activity exhibits highly robust responses to serum deprivation, which promotes cytoplasmic accumulation of YAP, and subsequent serum stimulation, which rapidly induces YAP nuclear translocation (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Serum stimulation rapidly induces YAP nuclear translocation.
source: In HEK293T cells, YAP activity exhibits highly robust responses to serum deprivation, which promotes cytoplasmic accumulation of YAP, and subsequent serum stimulation, which rapidly induces YAP nuclear translocation (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of full-length MAGI3 led to YAP cytoplasmic accumulation despite serum stimulated cell culture.
source: Consistent with the MAGI3 loss-of-function data, overexpression of full-length MAGI3 led to YAP cytoplasmic accumulation despite serum stimulated cell culture, whereas nuclear translocation of YAP was induced in untransfected control cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Nuclear translocation of YAP was induced in untransfected control cells under serum stimulation.
source: Consistent with the MAGI3 loss-of-function data, overexpression of full-length MAGI3 led to YAP cytoplasmic accumulation despite serum stimulated cell culture, whereas nuclear translocation of YAP was induced in untransfected control cells (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Expression of truncated MAGI3 caused increased nuclear YAP localization in cells even under serum deprived conditions.
source: By contrast, the expression of truncated MAGI3 caused the opposite effect by increasing nuclear YAP localization in cells even under the serum deprived conditions that normally preclude YAP from the nucleus (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The amount of phosphorylated/inactive YAP was reduced in lysates from cells expressing MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC-GFP compared to GFP control.
source: The increased nuclear YAP localization was indicative of heightened YAP activation, since the amount of phosphorylated/inactive YAP was reduced in lysates from cells expressing MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC-GFP compared to GFP control (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Truncated MAGI3 is positively associated with YAP activation.
source: Thus, in contrast to the inhibitory effect of full-length MAGI3 on YAP, these data demonstrate that truncated MAGI3 is positively associated with YAP activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the YAP localization and phosphorylation data.

claim: Knockdown of YAP in MCF10A-SV40 cells expressing MAGI3ΔC-GFP resulted in a significant reduction of colony formation on soft agar.
source: Indeed, knockdown of YAP in MCF10A-SV40 cells expressing MAGI3ΔC-GFP resulted in a significant reduction of colony formation on soft agar (p=7.4 x 10–5) (Figure 5F and G), suggesting that the increase in YAP activity caused by truncated MAGI3 is functionally important for transformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by soft agar assays shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The increase in YAP activity caused by truncated MAGI3 is functionally important for transformation.
source: Indeed, knockdown of YAP in MCF10A-SV40 cells expressing MAGI3ΔC-GFP resulted in a significant reduction of colony formation on soft agar (p=7.4 x 10–5) (Figure 5F and G), suggesting that the increase in YAP activity caused by truncated MAGI3 is functionally important for transformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis experiment showing YAP dependence of transformation.

claim: The presence of truncated MAGI3 was sufficient to prevent endogenous, full-length MAGI3 from interacting with YAP.
source: Indeed, the presence of truncated MAGI3 was sufficient to prevent endogenous, full-length MAGI3 from interacting with YAP (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Neither MAGI3pPA nor MAGI3ΔC-GFP was able to physically associate with YAP.
source: However, because both MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC-GFP lack the PDZ6 domain required for interaction with YAP (Figure 4D), neither truncation was able to physically associate with YAP (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: The absence of physical interaction between truncated MAGI3 and YAP demonstrates that truncated MAGI3 proteins do not directly compete with full-length MAGI3 for YAP binding.
source: The absence of physical interaction between truncated MAGI3 and YAP demonstrates that truncated MAGI3 proteins do not directly compete with full-length MAGI3 for YAP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing no interaction between truncated MAGI3 and YAP.

claim: Truncated and full-length MAGI3 proteins physically interact.
source: By co-immunoprecipitation, we found that truncated and full-length MAGI3 proteins do indeed physically interact (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: The ability of truncated MAGI3 proteins to form complexes with full-length MAGI3 interferes with physiological MAGI3/YAP interactions.
source: These results suggest that the ability of truncated MAGI3 proteins to form complexes with full-length MAGI3 interferes with physiological MAGI3/YAP interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing truncated MAGI3 interacts with full-length MAGI3 and prevents MAGI3/YAP interaction.

claim: The growth of tumors expressing high ratios of FL:pPA MAGI3 was significantly impaired compared to FL:pPA ratio-unmodified control tumors.
source: Consistent with the mechanism, the growth of tumors expressing high ratios of FL:pPA was significantly impaired compared to FL:pPA ratio-unmodified control tumors (p=5.8 x 10–5) (Figure 6F and G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by orthotopic xenograft experiments shown in Figure 6F and G.

claim: The recurrent MAGI3pPA product and other breast cancer-associated MAGI3 truncations suppress the inhibitory interaction between full-length MAGI3 and YAP.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that the recurrent MAGI3pPA product and other breast cancer-associated MAGI3 truncations suppress the inhibitory interaction between full-length MAGI3 and YAP, thus providing a molecular link between their dominant-negative activity and their oncogenic nature.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP and functional data showing dominant-negative mechanism.

claim: Oncogenic human papillomaviruses target MAGI3 for degradation.
source: For example, oncogenic human papillomaviruses, which have evolved to target critical tumor suppressors necessary for transformation such as p53, also target MAGI3 for degradation (Thomas et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MAGI3 was found to be part of a downregulated gene signature associated with breast tumor-initiating cells.
source: In addition, MAGI3 was found to be part of a downregulated gene signature associated with breast tumor-initiating cells (Creighton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MAGI3 is not frequently altered by nonsynonymous mutations or copy number losses in human cancer.
source: In human cancer, MAGI3 is not frequently altered by nonsynonymous mutations or copy number losses (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013), and has not been previously nominated as a driver.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cancer genomics databases, supported by citations.

claim: MAGI3 has not been previously nominated as a driver gene.
source: In human cancer, MAGI3 is not frequently altered by nonsynonymous mutations or copy number losses (Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013), and has not been previously nominated as a driver.
evidence: This is based on the literature and cancer genomics databases.

claim: The generation of truncated MAGI3 products by pPA or chromosomal rearrangement may more potently deregulate YAP activity and drive transformation compared to the mutation or loss of a single MAGI3 allele.
source: Moreover, the ability of these truncations to function as dominant-negative proteins and prevent the inhibition of YAP by full-length MAGI3 suggests that the generation of truncated MAGI3 products by pPA or chromosomal rearrangement may more potently deregulate YAP activity and drive transformation compared to the mutation or loss of a single MAGI3 allele.
evidence: This is speculated based on the dominant-negative mechanism.

claim: MAGI3 alterations in cancer may occur much more frequently than previously appreciated.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that MAGI3 alterations in cancer may occur much more frequently than previously appreciated and support the clinical relevance of MAGI3 truncations as driver alterations.
evidence: This is inferred from the recurrence data and functional studies.

claim: MAGI3 truncations are clinically relevant driver alterations.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that MAGI3 alterations in cancer may occur much more frequently than previously appreciated and support the clinical relevance of MAGI3 truncations as driver alterations.
evidence: This is inferred from the recurrence data and functional studies showing oncogenic properties.

claim: The C-terminal PDZ6 domain of MAGI3 is essential for MAGI3/YAP interaction.
source: Importantly, we found that the C-terminal PDZ6 domain of MAGI3 is essential for MAGI3/YAP interaction, whereas the two independent breast cancer-associated MAGI3 truncations studied here – MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC – lack this domain and fail to interact with YAP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments with deletion mutants (Figure 4D).

claim: MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC lack the PDZ6 domain and fail to interact with YAP.
source: Importantly, we found that the C-terminal PDZ6 domain of MAGI3 is essential for MAGI3/YAP interaction, whereas the two independent breast cancer-associated MAGI3 truncations studied here – MAGI3pPA and MAGI3ΔC – lack this domain and fail to interact with YAP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments (Figure 6B and C).

claim: MAGI3 truncations dominantly suppressed interactions between full-length MAGI3 and YAP, resulting in YAP activation and malignant transformation.
source: Nevertheless, the truncations dominantly suppressed interactions between full-length MAGI3 and YAP, resulting in YAP activation and malignant transformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments (Figure 6A) and transformation assays (Figures 3 and 5).

claim: MAGI3 truncations can physically associate with full-length MAGI3 proteins.
source: We further determined that MAGI3 truncations can physically associate with full-length MAGI3 proteins, and thus posit that this aberrant complex interferes with the interaction between full-length MAGI3 and YAP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments (Figure 6D and E).

claim: The aberrant complex between truncated and full-length MAGI3 interferes with the interaction between full-length MAGI3 and YAP.
source: We further determined that MAGI3 truncations can physically associate with full-length MAGI3 proteins, and thus posit that this aberrant complex interferes with the interaction between full-length MAGI3 and YAP.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing truncated MAGI3 interacts with full-length MAGI3 and prevents MAGI3/YAP interaction.

claim: The MAGI3/YAP interaction is important in suppressing malignant transformation.
source: Our results underscore the importance of the MAGI3/YAP interaction in suppressing malignant transformation and implicate MAGI3 as a new potential component involved in the regulation of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional studies showing that disruption of MAGI3/YAP interaction promotes transformation.

claim: MAGI3 is a new potential component involved in the regulation of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway.
source: Our results underscore the importance of the MAGI3/YAP interaction in suppressing malignant transformation and implicate MAGI3 as a new potential component involved in the regulation of the Hippo tumor suppressor pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing MAGI3 regulates YAP, a major Hippo pathway effector.

claim: In mantle cell lymphoma, mutations that generate novel, gene-proximal PAS in the CCND1 3′ UTR have been discovered.
source: In mantle cell lymphoma, for example, mutations that generate novel, gene-proximal PAS in the CCND1 3′ UTR have been discovered.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer mechanisms.

claim: In mantle cell lymphoma, the production of shorter, prematurely polyadenylated cyclin D1 mRNA isoforms, which exhibit dramatically extended half-lives, drive the overexpression of cyclin D1 oncoproteins.
source: In these tumors, the production of shorter, prematurely polyadenylated cyclin D1 mRNA isoforms, which exhibit dramatically extended half-lives, drive the overexpression of cyclin D1 oncoproteins (Wiestner et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Shorter 3′ UTRs utilizing the gene-proximal PAS are favored by cancer cells.
source: In addition, a number of studies on genes with tandem PAS arrangements in the 3′ UTR have shown that shorter 3′ UTRs utilizing the gene-proximal PAS are favored by cancer cells (Sandberg et al., 2008; Singh et al., 2009; Mayr and Bartel, 2009; Xia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Increased tendency in cancer cells to utilize gene-proximal PAS for cleavage and polyadenylation corresponds to increased mRNA half-life as well as protein expression.
source: This increased tendency in cancer cells to utilize gene-proximal PAS for cleavage and polyadenylation corresponds to increased mRNA half-life as well as protein expression (Singh et al., 2009; Mayr and Bartel, 2009), suggesting that 3′ UTR shortening may be a general mechanism of evading regulation by tumor suppressive microRNAs.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: 3′ UTR shortening may be a general mechanism of evading regulation by tumor suppressive microRNAs.
source: This increased tendency in cancer cells to utilize gene-proximal PAS for cleavage and polyadenylation corresponds to increased mRNA half-life as well as protein expression (Singh et al., 2009; Mayr and Bartel, 2009), suggesting that 3′ UTR shortening may be a general mechanism of evading regulation by tumor suppressive microRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on 3′ UTR shortening and its effects.

claim: In cancer, premature cleavage and polyadenylation can occur in the intron of a gene despite the absence of mutations in the immediate exon/intron sequences flanking the cryptic PAS.
source: Our study extends these previous findings by showing that, in cancer, premature cleavage and polyadenylation can occur in the intron of a gene despite the absence of mutations in the immediate exon/intron sequences flanking the cryptic PAS.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MAGI3 sequencing data showing no mutations.

claim: Alternative 3′ UTR PAS selection does not alter the mRNA coding potential.
source: While alternative 3′ UTR PAS selection does not alter the mRNA coding potential, pPA can cause gene-truncating alterations that produce pre-mRNAs with potential to encode constitutively active or dominant-negative proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RNA processing.

claim: pPA can cause gene-truncating alterations that produce pre-mRNAs with potential to encode constitutively active or dominant-negative proteins.
source: While alternative 3′ UTR PAS selection does not alter the mRNA coding potential, pPA can cause gene-truncating alterations that produce pre-mRNAs with potential to encode constitutively active or dominant-negative proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MAGI3pPA example in this study.

claim: pPA pre-mRNAs are naturally able to evade post-transcriptional quality-control surveillance mechanisms such as nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
source: Such pre-mRNAs are naturally able to evade post-transcriptional quality-control surveillance mechanisms such as nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of RNA surveillance mechanisms.

claim: pPA transcripts may cause significant functional and phenotypic consequences even if expressed at lower levels than wild-type mRNA isoforms.
source: By producing constitutively active or dominant-negative proteins, pPA transcripts may cause significant functional and phenotypic consequences even if expressed at lower levels than wild-type mRNA isoforms.
evidence: This is inferred from the MAGI3pPA data showing low expression but significant functional effects.

claim: U1 snRNP function is essential for protecting pre-mRNAs from pPA at cryptic intronic PAS.
source: For example, U1 snRNP function is essential for protecting pre-mRNAs from pPA at cryptic intronic PAS (Kaida et al., 2010; Almada et al., 2013), and experimental depletion of U1 snRNP levels can lead to the production of novel, pPA-truncated isoforms that encode dominant-negative proteins (Vorlová et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Experimental depletion of U1 snRNP levels can lead to the production of novel, pPA-truncated isoforms that encode dominant-negative proteins.
source: For example, U1 snRNP function is essential for protecting pre-mRNAs from pPA at cryptic intronic PAS (Kaida et al., 2010; Almada et al., 2013), and experimental depletion of U1 snRNP levels can lead to the production of novel, pPA-truncated isoforms that encode dominant-negative proteins (Vorlová et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of polyadenylation factors has been shown to mediate alternative intronic PAS usage.
source: Overexpression of polyadenylation factors has also been shown to mediate alternative intronic PAS usage (Takagaki et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The relative abundance of U1 snRNP to nuclear pre-mRNAs is a critical factor for determining whether global pPA events occur.
source: Moreover, because the relative abundance of U1 snRNP to nuclear pre-mRNAs is a critical factor for determining whether global pPA events occur (Berg et al., 2012), alterations that drive global transcriptional amplification, a phenomenon frequently observed in cancer cells (Nie et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014; Cunningham et al., 2014), might also induce pPA.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Global transcriptional amplification is a phenomenon frequently observed in cancer cells.
source: Moreover, because the relative abundance of U1 snRNP to nuclear pre-mRNAs is a critical factor for determining whether global pPA events occur (Berg et al., 2012), alterations that drive global transcriptional amplification, a phenomenon frequently observed in cancer cells (Nie et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014; Cunningham et al., 2014), might also induce pPA.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Alterations that drive global transcriptional amplification might induce pPA.
source: Moreover, because the relative abundance of U1 snRNP to nuclear pre-mRNAs is a critical factor for determining whether global pPA events occur (Berg et al., 2012), alterations that drive global transcriptional amplification, a phenomenon frequently observed in cancer cells (Nie et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2012; Sabò et al., 2014; Cunningham et al., 2014), might also induce pPA.
evidence: This is speculated based on the relationship between U1 snRNP abundance and pPA.
